# Remote-main collection and warm-refresh cutoff cache

Status: implemented and locally verified
Scope: Python collector, cache, CLI diagnostics, report provenance, macOS fallback notice, tests and docs; no scheduling change

## Problem and intended behavior

On a local Adastra refresh matching the app's 366-day collector request, the old CLI took 36.25 seconds despite 13/13 churn cache hits, 3,539 snapshot cache hits, and no snapshots to compute. The snapshot loop still launched `git log -1 --before=<cutoff> HEAD` for each repository and period before probing the snapshot cache. An isolated 185-day warm lookup pass took 18.6 seconds. During implementation, a 31-day warm run with cutoff caching still took 41.92 seconds because sequential best-effort fetch consumed 41.68 seconds and most remotes failed; a subsequent run with bounded four-way fetch took 15.46 seconds, with 14.05 seconds in fetch. The full isolated 366-day collection then completed in 264.10 seconds on a cold schema-5 cache; the next run took 16.20 seconds, with 4,758 cutoff cache hits, no cutoff queries, 3,539 snapshot cache hits and no snapshot work. These local samples used different remote states and source policies from the old 36.25-second run; they establish the warm path's behavior, not a controlled speedup guarantee.

The owner wants **all metrics based on each repository's `origin/main`, never its checked-out branch or detached HEAD**. The collector should best-effort fetch that branch on every run, including routine app refreshes; if fetch fails, use the last locally fetched `origin/main`. A fetch does not change the working tree or local branch. The remote-tracking ref is only as current as the last successful fetch: in the observed checkout, Adastra's local HEAD was two commits ahead of its locally stored `origin/main`.

**Compatibility decision:** Make this the collector's single default, including the public CLI, rather than silently mixing HEAD and remote-main reports or adding a second source mode. This is a breaking requirement for local-only repositories, `master`-default repositories, and counted submodules without `origin/main`; collection fails until that ref exists or the repository is excluded by workspace config. The README and release notes must state that requirement, and the error must name both remedies. The owner explicitly requested remote-main over local history; this trade-off is intentional, not an accidental failure path.

Success: a warm run against unchanged remote-tracking tips and the same cutoffs issues no per-cutoff Git queries. Churn, snapshots, and report provenance all correspond to the captured `origin/main` OID for each repository, including when a ref moves during a run. A failed fetch with an existing ref still produces a report from that ref and surfaces a concise warning; a missing ref never silently falls back to local HEAD.

## Source selection and fetch

For every counted repository, attempt a bounded, non-interactive fetch of remote `main` into its `refs/remotes/origin/main` before resolving the source OID. Use the forcing refspec `+refs/heads/main:refs/remotes/origin/main`: a remote force-push must update the local tracking ref rather than leave it permanently stuck on the old tip. Do not fetch all remotes or tags, check out a branch, reset, or alter submodule worktrees. Set `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` and disable Git askpass interaction for the fetch child; provide no stdin. Allow at most 8 seconds per fetch and 45 seconds of fetch attempts per workspace, running up to four independent repository fetches concurrently; these limits bound network delay, not total collection time (the app's routine per-workspace timeout remains 300 seconds). If the total budget expires, use existing refs for remaining repositories. Rotate the first attempted repository to the first budget-skipped repository on the next run, so a repeatedly unavailable early remote does not always starve later ones. Persist that repository identity with the workspace cache; if the repo disappears, start from the first current repository. With `--no-cache`, attempt repositories in discovery order and do not persist rotation. On POSIX, per-fetch timeouts and app cancellation signal the fetch process groups and their children; if the OS denies group termination, collection falls back to the last-fetched ref rather than crashing, but an inaccessible helper may outlive the timeout. On Windows the standard-library implementation can terminate the direct Git process but cannot promise child-process termination.

After each attempt, resolve `refs/remotes/origin/main` and pin its OID for the rest of that repository's collection. On network failure, authentication failure, or timeout, retain and use the last locally fetched OID. If the ref does not exist, fail the collection with an actionable error identifying the repository and missing ref; do not substitute `HEAD` or publish a partial new report. Do not print remote URLs, credential-helper output, or unredacted fetch stderr in diagnostics. The CLI and app use the same collector path. No new network tier, background service, or separate refresh API is needed.

Use the captured OID in **every Git history operation**: full churn log, incremental range (`cached_oid..current_oid`), and snapshot cutoff lookup. A force-push or rewind falls through the existing ancestry check to a full churn rescan. Count snapshots from the selected historical commit as before. If a selected commit becomes unavailable or any later Git churn, cutoff, archive, or snapshot-count operation fails, abort before writing HTML or JSON; do not convert that failure into zero churn or a missing snapshot. The app retains its previous saved report and shows the collection failure. Existing snapshot cache entries are still valid when their commit and counting policy match; churn cache entries record the selected source OID, not the checked-out HEAD. If an older cache entry happens to have that same OID, its churn is valid because the source history is the same.

Expose the source ref, captured tip OID, and fetch outcome (`fetched`, `failed`, or `budget_skipped`) per repository in additive version-1 JSON report metadata and in the CLI summary. The tip OID alone cannot distinguish a successful fetch from a last-fetched fallback. Decode the optional fields in the macOS app and surface fallback via its existing notice banner for both individual and aggregate scopes; old saved reports without these fields remain readable. In aggregate scope, append the fallback warning to any existing portfolio warning rather than replacing it. A successful collection with a fallback cannot rely on stderr alone, because the app discards collector output on success. CLI diagnostics identify the repository and say `fetch failed`, `timed out`, or `budget skipped`, with a suggestion to fetch manually for details. Do not relay raw Git stderr or remote URLs in either fetch or collection errors; these can contain credentials.

## Cutoff lookup cache

Use one canonical repository identity (resolved checkout path and Git directory) in **all three** cache keys: churn, snapshot, and cutoff lookup. A display label alone can be reassigned to a different checkout, and a cached count can depend on repository-path policy even at the same commit OID. The cutoff section groups entries by this identity, with the selected `origin/main` OID and a map from exact cutoff ISO string to commit OID or JSON `null`. Reuse an entry only when its stored source OID equals the OID captured after the fetch attempt; on a change, discard that repository's cutoff map. A new commit can be backdated, so even earlier cutoff answers must be invalidated. A stored `null` (no commit at that cutoff) differs from an absent key. A Git error is not cached.

On misses, keep `git log -1 --before=<cutoff>` but query the captured OID rather than the moving ref, and store the answer under that same OID. This avoids binding an answer from a concurrent ref update to the wrong cache key. Bulk timestamp sorting is not interchangeable with Git's traversal and cutoff semantics. `--no-cache` bypasses both persistent caches, not source selection or best-effort fetch.

Bump the private cache schema from 4 to 5 when the repository identity enters all cache keys. Old label-only entries cannot prove which checkout produced them and are not migrated; the first run is cold and may exceed the app's routine timeout, but the existing churn and snapshot checkpoints allow a later run to resume. The previously saved report remains available while the cache warms; a manual CLI run without the app timeout can prime it. Within schema 5, the cutoff section is optional and `load_cache` supplies an empty section when absent. Checkpoint lookups after the cutoff pass, before snapshot counting, so interrupted history extensions can resume. Existing atomic writes prevent partial files, but concurrent collectors may overwrite each other's new entries; that costs future hits, not report correctness.

Add a CLI timing line for fetch and cutoff lookup, plus cutoff hit/miss counts. Retain the existing churn and snapshot counters. The existing `work-tempo --root PATH --period day --days N --workers 2 --no-html` command remains the manual refresh entrypoint; the macOS app currently discards collector stdout, so timing lines are for CLI diagnosis.

## Verification

Use temporary Git repositories with distinct checked-out HEAD and `origin/main` to assert that **all** churn and snapshot totals follow the remote-tracking ref. Test successful fetch advancing the ref, failed fetch falling back to the stored ref and surfacing a notice, a counted repository with no ref causing a full collection failure without replacing the previous report, per-fetch timeout, total-budget fairness across runs, cancellation with child processes, and a forced ref rewind. Inject later churn, cutoff, and snapshot Git failures to prove they abort publication rather than produce partial totals. Keep network tests local with fixture remotes; no CI internet dependency.

Compare cold, warm and `--no-cache` reports; assert a warm run makes no per-cutoff `git log` calls. Cover cached `null`, a new cutoff, two checkouts sharing a display label and cache file, a backdated commit, rewritten history, and a ref moving between capture and lookup. Compare returned commits with the existing Git lookup at cutoff boundaries and with divergent author/committer dates; do not derive expectations by timestamp sorting. Verify schema-4 caches cold-start safely under schema 5 and the macOS report decoder accepts additive provenance. Benchmark the same Adastra CLI request before/after on a warm cache and report total, fetch, and cutoff-lookup durations separately; no hard CI timing threshold.

## Delivery sequence

First prove the bounded, non-interactive fetch against a local fixture remote, including a force-push and timed-out child process. Then switch all history reads to the pinned remote-tracking OID, unify repository identity across the existing caches (schema 5), add provenance, and make collection failures abort publication. Verify the app's existing report remains available on failure and its notice banner identifies a last-fetched fallback. Update the public CLI documentation and release notes for the strict `origin/main` requirement; slice 1 does not yet improve warm lookup speed. Then add the optional cutoff lookup cache and timing counters, with a separate warm-run benchmark. This keeps a source-correctness regression distinguishable from a cache regression.

## Boundaries

No change to metric definitions, refresh cadence, cache placement, counting policy, or snapshot extraction. A failed fetch falls back to **last fetched origin/main**, not to local HEAD; no fetched ref means an explicit failure. Git history modifications that leave the selected OID unchanged (for example replace refs or shallow-boundary changes) remain outside the cache guarantee, as with the existing churn cache. Any broader history fingerprint is a separate correctness decision.
